questions.q: Why does the lesson say landmark, heavily-cited papers are often worse reproduction targets than smaller, specific papers?
options: Landmark results often pushed the edge of available hardware/scale on access-restricted devices with engineering details not fully described in the main text
Landmark papers are usually written in a foreign language
Landmark papers never contain any experimental results
Journals forbid reproducing landmark papers
questions.explain: The lesson explains landmark papers frequently pushed the edge of available hardware at the time, often on access-restricted devices, with supplementary engineering not fully described -- making them harder, not easier, to reproduce.

questions.q: Which of the five screening checklist items addresses whether you can actually run the paper's experiment with resources available to you?
options: Resource match -- whether the paper's circuit fits hardware/simulators you can access
Age and citation context
Scope relative to your timeline
Availability of code or data
questions.explain: Resource match is specifically about whether the circuit fits public-access hardware or simulators (IBM Quantum open tier, Azure Quantum, Amazon Braket, Qiskit Aer) you can realistically use.

questions.q: In the worked three-candidate example, why was the theoretical complexity-bound paper rejected as a reproduction target?
options: It has no circuit implementation or experimental method at all -- it's pure theory, not an experimental claim to reproduce
Because it required more than 50 qubits
Because its code and data were unavailable
Because it was published too recently
questions.explain: The worked table marks it 'N/A, not an experimental method' -- there's no circuit or experiment to attempt, since the paper is purely theoretical.

questions.q: Per the lesson, what is a reasonable scope for a capstone-level reproduction target, relative to the whole original paper?
options: A single figure or a single table's main result, not the paper's entire set of experiments
Every single experiment and figure in the paper, in full
Only the paper's abstract and title
A completely unrelated experiment inspired loosely by the paper's topic
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly states a capstone-appropriate target is usually a single figure or table's main result, not the entire paper's experimental scope.

questions.q: If a paper used a proprietary, access-restricted device, what does the lesson suggest as a legitimate alternative, with an important caveat?
options: A noiseless-simulator version of the same circuit, explicitly framed as reproducing the algorithmic claim rather than the hardware-noise behavior
Abandoning any reproduction attempt entirely, since no alternative exists
Using the exact same proprietary device without permission
Claiming the simulator result is identical to the original hardware result with no caveat
questions.explain: The lesson states a simulator version is still a legitimate target, but you must be explicit that you're testing the algorithmic claim, not the hardware-noise behavior the original paper measured.
